name: astroterm
why: A terminal planetarium renders real sky positions, turning astronomy into something you can watch and explore.

brief.what_it_is: astroterm is a terminal-based star map written in C. It draws the real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations and the moon as ASCII (optionally Unicode, braille, and colour) inside your terminal. You give it an observer latitude and longitude, or a city name, and a date and time in UTC, or it uses the system clock. It then renders the sky for that place and time, and can animate it at a chosen speed.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches it as a way to explore the sky without a telescope: 'no telescope required!' It is meant for choosing any date, time and location to look at past, present or future celestial events. The README also says the project is 'constantly improving' and invites ideas and bug reports through issues.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internals in detail. It credits a list of astronomy sources for the math, including Meeus-style solar position work, Paul Schlyter's planetary position method, JPL approximate planetary positions, and Greg Miller's RA/Dec to Alt/Az conversion. Star data comes from the Yale Bright Star Catalog (BSC5). Constellation figures come from Stellarium's modern sky culture, converted to BSC5 indices. City coordinates come from GeoNames. The README also says it uses 'ASCII-rendered visuals' with a terminal cell aspect ratio that can be overridden with --aspect-ratio.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is one of several options. Others are Arch (pacman), Fedora 40+ (dnf), Nix (nix-shell for a trial run, or configuration.nix), and Guix (guix shell or guix package --install, pinned to a specific commit via time-machine). Unix users can download a prebuilt binary with wget from the releases page, using os darwin or linux and arch x86_64 or aarch64; curl does not follow the latest-release redirect, so wget is recommended. Windows users can use PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest to get astroterm-win-x86_64.exe. Building from source is described in CONTRIBUTING.md. For a Unicode display on Linux, the README says to set LC_ALL and LC_CTYPE to en_US.UTF-8 and configure the locales package. No accounts, API keys or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a planetarium that runs inside a terminal and renders real ephemeris positions. You can scrub to any historical date, such as the Apollo 11 morning, and check the result against Stellarium, which the README does. Its own features are the constellation stick figures drawn in braille and an optional azimuthal grid.
brief.status: maintained. The latest release is v1.2.0, marked 'Latest', dated '01 Apr' on the releases page (the year is not shown in the scraped text). Before it: v1.1.0 on 29 Mar, v1.0.10 on 16 Jan, v1.0.9 on 29 Aug, and several more in the 1.0.x line. The README has a CI test badge and a codecov badge, and it links to a Repology packaging badge showing the project is in several distros. The release notes show several outside contributors. The README does not contain an explicit maintenance statement.
brief.caveats: The README says arm64 Linux binaries are 'to come' after Ubuntu arm64 runners are available, so only x86_64 Linux prebuilt binaries are offered for now. Unicode and braille output depend on the terminal's locale and font, and the README includes a troubleshooting section for that. Locations near the poles look different because star motion is more circular there. Constellation figures are drawn only when every star in the figure is above the magnitude threshold. The license is MIT, per the badge. The README does not describe a Windows build beyond the .exe download. Building from source is pointed at CONTRIBUTING.md, which I did not open.
